title: Microsoft 365 outage traced to a July gateway bug, a Teams traffic shift and 14% missing capacity
verification: Ars Technica (Nov 16) and Office Watch (Nov 16), both from Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report (dated Nov 15; incidents EX1550543, MO1550821): outage Nov 12 16:20 UTC to Nov 13 16:10 UTC (just under 24 h; 11:20 a.m. ET start); most users could not reach mailboxes in Outlook, Outlook on the web, mobile mail; Teams mostly worked. Three causes: a Windows fix for gateway servers rolled out starting in July caused lockups under heavy load on newer, high-core-count hardware, missed in pre-release testing on less powerful hardware, ran over three months without trouble; Teams traffic moved onto the Exchange gateway about 15 h before (1:07 a.m. UTC); about 14% of gateway capacity out from an unrelated fault. Automatic rerouting spread lockups; over 80% of servers unresponsive within under two hours; regional isolation failed. Restarted servers were swamped by queued requests; rollbacks could not quickly revert months-old change; fix was a targeted update restoring the earlier code, rolled out in batches (Asia Pacific, then Europe). Microsoft: 'not related to cyber or AI/agents'. Final report due Nov 20. Incoming mail got extra time so it did not bounce.

slides.headline: A bug hid for three months. Then Outlook went dark.

image.credit: Photo: a Microsoft data center. Robert Scoble / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

slides.text: On November 12, Microsoft's work email broke around the world. For almost 24 hours, most users couldn't open their inbox in Outlook.

image.credit: Photo: a Microsoft data center in Sweden. Johan Wessman / News Oresund / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

slides.text: Microsoft's report blames three small problems at once. First: a fix sent to its gateway servers in July hid a bug. Tests missed it because the test machines were weaker.

image.credit: Photo: Microsoft's campus in Redmond, Washington, 2009. Jelson25 / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

slides.text: Second: about 14% of those servers were already down from an unrelated fault. Third: Teams traffic had been moved onto the same servers 15 hours earlier.
Under the extra load, servers froze. Their traffic moved to the next ones, which froze too. In under two hours, more than 80% were stuck.

image.credit: Illustrative photo: a server rack. Kim Scarborough / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

slides.text: Restarting didn't help. Piled-up requests swamped each server the moment it came back. Engineers had to push a fix, region by region.

image.credit: Photo: Microsoft's Azure data center in Wenatchee, Washington. Tedder / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

slides.text: Microsoft says it was not a hack and not AI. Its full report is due November 20. Send this to whoever had to answer “Is email down?” all day.

caption:
The bug had been running quietly on Microsoft's servers since July. It only needed a busy afternoon.

On November 12, starting at about 11:20 a.m. Eastern, most Microsoft 365 users could not open their mailboxes in Outlook, on the web or on their phones. It lasted just under 24 hours. Teams mostly kept working.

Microsoft's preliminary report names three problems that hit together. A fix for its gateway servers, the front door to its cloud, carried a bug that locked up newer, more powerful machines under heavy load. Testing missed it because the test hardware was weaker. About 14% of gateway capacity was already out from an unrelated fault. And about 15 hours earlier, Teams traffic had been shifted onto the gateway that also serves email.

As the US workday peaked, servers froze. Automatic rerouting pushed their traffic onto healthy servers, which then froze too. More than 80% were stuck within two hours, and the walls meant to keep a failure inside one region did not hold.

Restarts failed because queued requests swamped each server instantly. A simple rollback was not possible either, because the change was months old. Engineers wrote a targeted fix and rolled it out in batches.

Incoming mail was held, not bounced. The final report is due November 20.

Source: Microsoft's preliminary report, via Ars Technica and Office Watch
